**Fußballclub Gelsenkirchen-Schalke 04 e. V.**, commonly known as **Schalke 04** (German:[[ˌʃalkə nʊl ˈfiːɐ̯]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Standard_German "Help:IPA/Standard German")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/e2/De-Schalke_04.ogg/De-Schalke_04.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:De-Schalke_04.ogg "File:De-Schalke 04.ogg")) and abbreviated as **S04** (German:[[ˈɛs nʊl fiːɐ̯]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Standard_German "Help:IPA/Standard German")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/8/87/De-S04.ogg/De-S04.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:De-S04.ogg "File:De-S04.ogg")), is a [professional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professionalism_in_association_football "Professionalism in association football")[sports club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_club "Sports club") from the [Schalke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelsenkirchen-Schalke "Gelsenkirchen-Schalke") district of [Gelsenkirchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelsenkirchen "Gelsenkirchen"), North Rhine-Westphalia. It is best known for its [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") team, which plays in the [Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundesliga "Bundesliga"), the top flight of the [German football league system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_football_league_system "German football league system"), following [promotion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promotion_and_relegation "Promotion and relegation") from the [2. Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2._Bundesliga "2. Bundesliga") in [2025–26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_2._Bundesliga "2025–26 2. Bundesliga"). Other activities offered by the club include [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_of_athletics "Sport of athletics"), [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball"), [handball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_handball "Team handball"), [table tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_tennis "Table tennis"), [winter sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_sport "Winter sport") and [eSports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESports "ESports").

The "04" in the club's name derives from its formation in 1904. Schalke have been one of the most popular professional [football teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_team "Football team") in Germany, even though the club's heyday was in the 1930s and 1940s. As of September 2025, the club has 210,000 members,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-2) making it the third-largest football club in Germany and the [sixth-largest club in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sports_clubs_by_membership "List of sports clubs by membership") in terms of membership.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-:2-3)

Schalke have won seven [German championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_German_football_champions "List of German football champions"), five [DFB-Pokals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DFB-Pokal "DFB-Pokal"), one [DFB Ligapokal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DFB_Ligapokal "DFB Ligapokal"), one [DFL-Supercup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DFL-Supercup "DFL-Supercup"), one [UEFA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Europa_League "UEFA Europa League") and two [UEFA Intertoto Cups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Intertoto_Cup "UEFA Intertoto Cup"). In 1937, Schalke became the first German club to win [the double](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_(association_football) "Double (association football)"). Since 2001, Schalke's stadium has been the [Veltins-Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_AufSchalke "Arena AufSchalke"). Schalke hold a long-standing rivalry with [Ruhr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruhr "Ruhr") neighbors [Borussia Dortmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borussia_Dortmund "Borussia Dortmund"), known as the [Revierderby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revierderby "Revierderby").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=FC_Schalke_04&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [List of FC Schalke 04 seasons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_FC_Schalke_04_seasons "List of FC Schalke 04 seasons")

### 1904–1927: Schalke's early years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=FC_Schalke_04&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1904–1927: Schalke's early years")]

[![Image 43](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F015017-0006%2C_Zeche_Bergmannsgl%C3%BCck%2C_Gelsenkirchen-Buer.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F015017-0006%2C_Zeche_Bergmannsgl%C3%BCck%2C_Gelsenkirchen-Buer.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F015017-0006,_Gelsenkirchen-Buer,_Kohlebergbau.jpg)

1900s typical mining structure in the Ruhr, source of the Schalke nickname Die Knappen – from an old German word for "miners"– because the team drew so many of its players and supporters from the coalmine workers of Gelsenkirchen.

The club was founded on 4 May 1904 as **Westfalia Schalke** by a group of high school students and first wore the colours red and yellow.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The team was unable to gain admittance[_[why?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] to the _[Westdeutscher Spielverband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western\_German\_Football\_Association "Western German Football Association") (Western German Football Association)_ and played in one of the "wild associations" of early German football. In 1912, after years of failed attempts to join the official league,[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] they merged with the gymnastic club **Schalker Turnverein 1877** in order to facilitate their entry. This arrangement held up until 1915, when **SV Westfalia Schalke** was re-established as an independent club. The separation proved short-lived and the two came together again in 1919 as **Turn- und Sportverein Schalke 1877**. The new club won its first honours in 1923 as champions of the _Schalke Kreisliga_. It was around this time that Schalke picked up the nickname _Die Knappen_, from an old German word for "miners" because the team drew so many of its players and supporters from the coal miners of Gelsenkirchen.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1924, the football team parted ways with the gymnasts again,[_[why?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] this time taking the club chairman along with them. They took the name **FC Schalke 04** and adopted the now familiar blue and white [kit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kit_(association_football) "Kit (association football)") from which their second nickname would derive, _Die Königsblauen_ (English: The Royal Blues). The following year, the club became the dominant local side, based on a style of play that used short, sharp, man-to-man passing to move the ball. This system would later become famous as the _Schalker Kreisel_ (English: spinning top; gyroscope).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In 1927, it carried them into the top-flight _Gauliga Ruhr_, onto the league championship, and then into the opening rounds of the national finals. [_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### 1928–1933: Rise to dominance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=FC_Schalke_04&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1928–1933: Rise to dominance")]

Following the club's initial success, it quickly gained in popularity, especially among the working class.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-Kuster2010-4) In 1928, the club built a new stadium, the Glückauf-Kampfbahn, and acknowledged the city's support by renaming themselves **FC Gelsenkirchen-Schalke 04**. They won their first West German championship in 1929,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-5) but the following year were sanctioned for exceeding salary levels set by the league and, in an era that considered professionalism in sport to be anathema, found themselves banned from play for nearly half a year.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

However, the ban had little impact on the team's popularity: in their first match after the ban against [Fortuna Düsseldorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortuna_D%C3%BCsseldorf "Fortuna Düsseldorf"), in June 1931, the team drew 70,000 spectators to its home ground. The club's fortunes begun to rise from 1931 and they made a semi-final appearance in the [1932 German championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1932_German_football_championship "1932 German football championship"), losing 1–2 to [Eintracht Frankfurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eintracht_Frankfurt "Eintracht Frankfurt"). [The year after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1933_German_football_championship "1933 German football championship"), the club reached the final, where Fortuna Düsseldorf proved the better side, winning 3–0.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-6)

### 1933–1945: The championship years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=FC_Schalke_04&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1933–1945: The championship years")]

With the re-organisation of German football in 1933 under [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany"), Schalke were placed in the [Gauliga Westfalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauliga_Westfalen "Gauliga Westfalen"), 1 of 16 top-flight divisions established to replace the innumerable regional and local leagues, all claiming top status. This league saw Schalke's most successful decade in their history: from 1933 to 1942, the club would appear in 14 of 18 national finals (ten in the German championship and eight in the [Tschammerpokal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tschammerpokal#Tschammer-Pokal "Tschammerpokal"), the predecessor of today's [DFB-Pokal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DFB-Pokal "DFB-Pokal")) and win their league in every one of its eleven seasons.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The club never lost a home match in the Gauliga Westfalen in all these 11 seasons and only lost six away matches, while remaining unbeaten in the 1935–36, 1936–37, 1937–38, 1938–39, 1940–41 and 1942–43 seasons, a sign of the club's dominance.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-7)

[![Image 44](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-2004-1001-503%2C_Berlin%2C_Zuschauer_beim_Fu%C3%9Fball-Endspiel.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-2004-1001-503%2C_Berlin%2C_Zuschauer_beim_Fu%C3%9Fball-Endspiel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-2004-1001-503,_Berlin,_Zuschauer_beim_Fu%C3%9Fball-Endspiel.jpg)

FC Schalke 04 supporters in 1941  
(Score table says "Kriegsmeistershaft" - "War championship")

Schalke's first [national title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_German_football_champions#German_football_championships_in_Nazi_Germany_(1933%E2%80%9345) "List of German football champions") came in [1934](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1934_German_football_championship "1934 German football championship") with a 2–1 victory over favourites [1. FC Nürnberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_N%C3%BCrnberg "1. FC Nürnberg"). [The next year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_German_football_championship "1935 German football championship"), they successfully defended their title against [VfB Stuttgart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VfB_Stuttgart "VfB Stuttgart") with a 6–4 win. The club missed the [1936](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_German_football_championship "1936 German football championship") final, but would make appearances in the championship match in each of the next six years, coming away victorious in [1937](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1937_German_football_championship "1937 German football championship"), [1939](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1939_German_football_championship "1939 German football championship"), [1940](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1940_German_football_championship "1940 German football championship") and [1942](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1942_German_football_championship "1942 German football championship"). Three of those national finals were against Austrian teams – [Admira Wien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VfB_Admira_Wacker_M%C3%B6dling "VfB Admira Wacker Mödling"), [Rapid Wien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SK_Rapid_Wien "SK Rapid Wien") and [First Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Vienna_FC "First Vienna FC") – which played in Germany's Gauliga Ostmark after Austria's incorporation into the Reich through the 1938 _[Anschluss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anschluss "Anschluss")_.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

_Die Königsblauen_ also made frequent appearances in the final of the Tschammerpokal, but had less success there. They lost the [inaugural Tschammerpokal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_Tschammerpokal "1935 Tschammerpokal") 0–2 to 1. FC Nürnberg in 1935. They also made failed appearances in the [1936](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Tschammerpokal "1936 Tschammerpokal"), [1941](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1941_Tschammerpokal "1941 Tschammerpokal"), and [1942](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1942_Tschammerpokal "1942 Tschammerpokal") finals with their only victory coming in [1937](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1937_Tschammerpokal "1937 Tschammerpokal") against Fortuna Düsseldorf.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Over a dozen seasons, from 1933 to 1945, Schalke won 162 of 189 Gauliga matches, drawing 21 and losing only 6. Within this period, they scored 924 goals and conceded just 145. From 1935 to 1939, they did not lose a single league match. The club's dominance throughout this period led them to be held up for propaganda purposes by the [Nazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazism "Nazism") regime as an example of "new Germany".[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### 1945–1959: Football after World War II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=FC_Schalke_04&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1945–1959: Football after World War II")]

[![Image 45](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Kuzorra87.jpg/250px-Kuzorra87.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kuzorra87.jpg)

Commonly regarded as the greatest S04 player of all time alongside [Fritz Szepan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Szepan "Fritz Szepan"), [Ernst Kuzorra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Kuzorra "Ernst Kuzorra") is also commonly regarded as one of the greatest German [forwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward_(association_football) "Forward (association football)") and led S04 to become the dominant team in [German football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_in_Germany "Football in Germany") winning six [German championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_German_football_champions "List of German football champions") and one [DFB-Pokal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DFB-Pokal "DFB-Pokal") from 1934 to 1942. [Ernst Kuzorra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Kuzorra "Ernst Kuzorra") was one of the main axes of what became known as the "**Schalker Kreisel**; a system that used quick and short [passing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passing_(association_football) "Passing (association football)")", to confuse and overwhelm the opponent.

With Germany in chaos towards the end of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Schalke played just two matches in 1945. They resumed regular play following the war and, for a few years, continued to compete as a strong side. They set a record in a national championship round match with a 20–0 win against [SpVgg Herten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2._Oberliga_West#Overview "2. Oberliga West"), but that spoke more to the weakened condition of German football than to the ability of the team.[_[according to whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] Schalke's play fell off, and they only finished sixth in the new Oberliga West in 1947. Within two years, they slipped to 12th place.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

It would take Schalke until the mid-1950s to recover their form. They finished third in a tight three-way race for the 1954 Oberliga West title, decided on the last day of the season. The following year, they appeared in the [DFB-Pokal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1954%E2%80%9355_DFB-Pokal "1954–55 DFB-Pokal") final, where they lost 2–3 to [Karlsruher SC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlsruher_SC "Karlsruher SC"). The club's next, and to date last, German championship came in [1958](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_football_championship_1958 "German football championship 1958") with a 3–0 victory over [Hamburger SV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburger_SV "Hamburger SV"). The strong fanbase of the club is as well documented in a local church, St. Joseph, in Gelsenkirchen. It was renovated shortly after the 1958 victory, where one of the glass windows shows [Aloysius Gonzaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aloysius_Gonzaga "Aloysius Gonzaga") with a football and the dress and colours of Schalke.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-8)

### 1960–2000: Entry to the Bundesliga and the _Euro Fighters_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=FC_Schalke_04&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1960–2000: Entry to the Bundesliga and the Euro Fighters")]

Schalke continued to play well, having several top four finishes in the years leading up to the 1963 formation of the [Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundesliga "Bundesliga"), West Germany's new federal, professional league. Those results earned them selection as 1 of 16 clubs admitted to the top-flight league.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Their first years in the Bundesliga were difficult. In [1964–65](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964%E2%80%9365_Bundesliga "1964–65 Bundesliga"), they escaped relegation only through the expansion of the league to 18 teams. A number of finishes at the lower end of the league table followed, before a marked improvement in [1971–72](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971%E2%80%9372_Bundesliga "1971–72 Bundesliga"), culminating in a second-place finish to [Bayern Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Bayern_Munich "FC Bayern Munich") and after having led the league for much of the season. In the same season, Schalke won the [DFB-Pokal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971%E2%80%9372_DFB-Pokal "1971–72 DFB-Pokal") for the second time in its history.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Despite their improved results, the seeds of a major reversal had already been sown. A number of the team's players and officials were accused of accepting [bribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bribes#Sport_corruption "Bribes") as part of the widespread [Bundesliga scandal of 1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundesliga_scandal_(1971) "Bundesliga scandal (1971)"). Investigation showed that Schalke had deliberately played to lose their 17 May, 28th-round match against [Arminia Bielefeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arminia_Bielefeld "Arminia Bielefeld"), 0–1. As a result, several Schalke players were banned for life, including three – [Klaus Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klaus_Fischer "Klaus Fischer"), ["Stan" Libuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinhard_Libuda "Reinhard Libuda") and [Klaus Fichtel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klaus_Fichtel "Klaus Fichtel") – who regularly played for the [West Germany national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_national_football_team "Germany national football team") at the time.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-10)

Even though the penalties were later commuted to bans ranging from six months to two years, the scandal had a profound effect on what might have possibly become one of the dominant German teams of the 1970s.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In 1973, the club moved to the [Parkstadion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkstadion "Parkstadion"), newly built for the [1974 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_FIFA_World_Cup "1974 FIFA World Cup") and having a capacity of 70,000 spectators. In the wake of the scandal, the club's performance was uneven. They managed another second-place result in [1976–77](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976%E2%80%9377_Bundesliga "1976–77 Bundesliga"), finishing just one point behind champions [Borussia Mönchengladbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borussia_M%C3%B6nchengladbach "Borussia Mönchengladbach").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In the early 1980s, _Die Knappen_ ran into trouble[_[tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing\_better\_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles")_] and were relegated to the [second division of the Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2._Bundesliga "2. Bundesliga") for the 1981–82 season and, after promotion, again in 1983–84. They returned to the top flight in [1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984%E2%80%9385_Bundesliga "1984–85 Bundesliga") but were relegated once more to the second tier in 1988. They returned to the Bundesliga in the [1991–92](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991%E2%80%9392_Bundesliga "1991–92 Bundesliga") season and stayed in the top flight until 2021.

[![Image 46](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Internazionale-Schalke_04_1997-05-21.svg/250px-Internazionale-Schalke_04_1997-05-21.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Internazionale-Schalke_04_1997-05-21.svg)

FC Schalke 04 starting line-up in their victorious [1997 UEFA Cup Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_UEFA_Cup_Final "1997 UEFA Cup Final").

The club earned their first honours since the DFB-Pokal win of 1972 with a victory in the final of the [1996–97 UEFA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996%E2%80%9397_UEFA_Cup "1996–97 UEFA Cup") over [Inter Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter_Milan "Inter Milan") on penalties. Coached by the Dutch coach [Huub Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huub_Stevens "Huub Stevens"), the 1997 Schalke squad earned the nickname "Euro Fighters", which is still in use among fans.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Stevens, who was widely unknown in Germany at the time, quickly earned himself a cult following among the Schalke supporters.

Stevens successfully implemented a system of rigid discipline, especially in the defence. His motto "_Die Null muß stehen_" (in [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language"), "It has to read nil"), which emphasized his importance on his side not conceding any goals, has found its way into everyday language in Germany.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### 2000–2019: Top-table mainstay, European semi-final

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=FC_Schalke_04&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2000–2019: Top-table mainstay, European semi-final")]

[![Image 47](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Schalke_04_Fans_664.jpg/250px-Schalke_04_Fans_664.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Schalke_04_Fans_664.jpg)

Fans displaying their colours at the [Veltins-Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_AufSchalke "Arena AufSchalke")

During the 1990s and early 2000, the club underwent a transformation into a modern, commercial sports organization and established itself as one of the dominant teams of the Bundesliga. Schalke won consecutive DFB-Pokals in [2000–01](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000%E2%80%9301_DFB-Pokal "2000–01 DFB-Pokal") and [2001–02](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001%E2%80%9302_DFB-Pokal "2001–02 DFB-Pokal"), and earned second-place finishes in the Bundesliga in [2000–01](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000%E2%80%9301_Bundesliga "2000–01 Bundesliga"), [2004–05](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004%E2%80%9305_Bundesliga "2004–05 Bundesliga") and [2006–07](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006%E2%80%9307_Bundesliga "2006–07 Bundesliga"). The [2000–01](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000%E2%80%9301_FC_Schalke_04_season "2000–01 FC Schalke 04 season") season finish was heartbreaking for Schalke's supporters as it took a goal in the fourth minute of injury time by Bayern Munich away to Hamburger SV to snatch the title from _Die Königsblauen_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-11)

Schalke finished in second place in 2005, a result that led to Schalke making its second appearance in the [UEFA Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005%E2%80%9306_UEFA_Champions_League "2005–06 UEFA Champions League"). There, Schalke finished in third place during the group stage and continuing into the [UEFA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005%E2%80%9306_UEFA_Cup "2005–06 UEFA Cup"), where they were eliminated by the eventual winners [Sevilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sevilla_FC "Sevilla FC") in the semi-finals. In [2005–06](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005%E2%80%9306_Bundesliga "2005–06 Bundesliga"), Schalke finished in fourth place in the Bundesliga, narrowly missing out on a Champions League spot. In [2006–07](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006%E2%80%9307_Bundesliga "2006–07 Bundesliga"), Schalke came agonizingly close to their first-ever Bundesliga title, finishing runners-up for the third time in seven seasons. They led much of the campaign, but a 2–0 away loss to rivals [Borussia Dortmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borussia_Dortmund "Borussia Dortmund") on the penultimate matchday left them second, just two points behind [VfB Stuttgart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VfB_Stuttgart "VfB Stuttgart").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-12)

In the [2007–08 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007%E2%80%9308_UEFA_Champions_League "2007–08 UEFA Champions League"), Schalke progressed past the [Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League "UEFA Champions League") group stage for the first time and advanced to the quarter-finals after defeating [Porto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Porto "FC Porto") on penalties in the round of 16. They were eliminated by [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Barcelona "FC Barcelona") in the quarter-finals, losing both home and away matches 0–1.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-13)

On 9 October 2006, Russian oil company [Gazprom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazprom "Gazprom") became the club's new sponsor. The company stated it expected to invest as much as €125 million in the club over a five-and-a-half-year period.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-14) Gazprom's sponsorship has been seen by some analysts as a politically motivated attempt to buy friendship in Germany.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-15) Within this sponsorship, Schalke 04 and [Zenit Saint Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Zenit_Saint_Petersburg "FC Zenit Saint Petersburg") signed a "partnership agreement"; both clubs intended to work closely on improving football-related issues.

On 13 April 2008, the club announced the dismissal of manager [Mirko Slomka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirko_Slomka "Mirko Slomka") after a heavy defeat at the hands[_[tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing\_better\_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles")_] of [Werder Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SV_Werder_Bremen "SV Werder Bremen") and elimination from the Champions League. Former players [Mike Büskens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_B%C3%BCskens "Mike Büskens") and [Youri Mulder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youri_Mulder "Youri Mulder") were put in charge of the first team on an interim basis. For the [2008–09 Bundesliga season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008%E2%80%9309_Bundesliga "2008–09 Bundesliga"), Schalke signed a new head coach, [Fred Rutten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Rutten "Fred Rutten"), previously of [Twente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Twente "FC Twente"). Rutten signed a contract running until June 2010.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-16) In March 2009, Rutten was sacked, and, once more, Mike Büskens, Youri Mulder and Oliver Reck took over the helm.

[![Image 48](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Raul_2011-08-03-2.jpg/250px-Raul_2011-08-03-2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raul_2011-08-03-2.jpg)

[Raúl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ra%C3%BAl_(footballer) "Raúl (footballer)"), then all-time top goalscorer in European club competitions, played for Schalke from 2010 to 2012

On 1 July 2009, [Felix Magath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Magath "Felix Magath"), who had led [VfL Wolfsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VfL_Wolfsburg "VfL Wolfsburg") to the top of the table in the Bundesliga, became head coach and general manager of the _Königsblauen_. The appointment of Magath as manager coincided with a multimillion-euro spending spree, allowing Schalke to acquire internationally known forwards [Klaas-Jan Huntelaar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klaas-Jan_Huntelaar "Klaas-Jan Huntelaar") and [Raúl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ra%C3%BAl_(footballer) "Raúl (footballer)"). Magath's tenure at the club was initially successful, seeing the side score a lot of goals in the first few months of the season, though defensive frailties and Magath's questionable squad selection had made him unpopular with Schalke supporters by December 2010.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

On 16 March 2011, Magath was sacked, and replaced with [Ralf Rangnick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralf_Rangnick "Ralf Rangnick"), who previously, between 2004 and 2005, had a brief spell being in charge of the team. Within just weeks of his appointment, Rangnick masterminded a 5–2 victory over Inter Milan at the [San Siro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Siro "San Siro") during the [quarter-finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010%E2%80%9311_UEFA_Champions_League_knockout_phase "2010–11 UEFA Champions League knockout phase") of the Champions League. Schalke advanced to the [semi-final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010%E2%80%9311_UEFA_Champions_League#Semi-finals "2010–11 UEFA Champions League") where they lost 2–0 to [Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C.") in the first leg and 4–1 in the second leg.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-17) However, Schalke 04 managed to win the [2010–11 DFB-Pokal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010%E2%80%9311_DFB-Pokal "2010–11 DFB-Pokal") after thrashing [MSV Duisburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MSV_Duisburg "MSV Duisburg") 5–0.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-18) On 1 June 2011, Schalke's captain, [Manuel Neuer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Neuer "Manuel Neuer"), made his move to Bayern Munich.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-19)

On 22 September 2011, Ralf Rangnick announced his immediate resignation as head coach of Schalke 04 due to [long-term exhaustion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnout_(psychology) "Burnout (psychology)").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-20) Assistant coach Seppo Eichkorn coached the team as interim manager until the appointment of Huub Stevens on 27 September 2011. Stevens' contract was to run until 30 June 2013.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-21)

[![Image 49](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Schalke04_Barcelona_CL0708_02.jpg/250px-Schalke04_Barcelona_CL0708_02.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Schalke04_Barcelona_CL0708_02.jpg)

FC Schalke 04 in the UEFA Champions League line-up against [FC Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Barcelona "FC Barcelona")

Despite having legendary[_[tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing\_better\_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles")_] status among Schalke supporters, Stevens's return to Schalke was met with some scepticism,[_[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] as fans feared that Stevens, who coached Schalke to the 1997 UEFA Cup win with a rigidly defensive system, could abandon Rangnick's system of attacking play in favour of returning to his 1997 defensive antics.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-22) The doubts of the supporters proved unfounded. Although Schalke played a somewhat inconsistent season, they reached third place in the Bundesliga and therefore direct qualification for the UEFA Champions League.

Schalke had an excellent start to the [2012–13 Bundesliga season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Bundesliga "2012–13 Bundesliga"), and worked their way to second place in the league by November, just behind Bayern Munich. On 20 October, Schalke traveled to [Borussia Dortmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borussia_Dortmund "Borussia Dortmund") for matchday 8, and defeated the home side 2–1 to secure their first league _[Revierderby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revierderby "Revierderby")_ win since February 2010 while securing a Champions League place by finishing in fourth place. In the [2013–14 UEFA Champions League group stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013%E2%80%9314_UEFA_Champions_League_group_stage "2013–14 UEFA Champions League group stage"), Schalke's opponents were [FCSB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FCSB "FCSB"), [FC Basel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Basel "FC Basel") and [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_F.C. "Chelsea F.C."). Schalke ultimately finished the group stage in second place, behind Chelsea, and was eliminated in the round of 16 by [Real Madrid CF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Madrid_CF "Real Madrid CF").

The most prominent Schalke addition was the arrival of [Kevin-Prince Boateng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin-Prince_Boateng "Kevin-Prince Boateng") from [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A.C._Milan "A.C. Milan").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-Schalke_sign_Kevin_Prince_Boateng-23) After a disappointing first round of the 2013–14 Bundesliga that saw Schalke in seventh place in the Bundesliga table, as well as an early exit from the [2013–14 DFB-Pokal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013%E2%80%9314_DFB-Pokal "2013–14 DFB-Pokal") in the first knockout round, the club played their most successful second half of the season in club history. The season was marked by numerous injuries to key squad players, including [Jefferson Farfán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Farf%C3%A1n "Jefferson Farfán") and Klaas-Jan Huntelaar, for almost the entire season. It also led to performance related discussions[_[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] about head coach Jens Keller. Partially, Schalke fielded up to ten young players with potential who played in the Schalke youth system throughout the season. Among the most promising young player discoveries of the 2013–14 season were [Max Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Meyer_(footballer) "Max Meyer (footballer)") and [Leon Goretzka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_Goretzka "Leon Goretzka"). The young Schalke squad won 11 out of 17 matches, totaling 36 points. At the end of the 2013–14 season, the club finished in third place in the Bundesliga table to qualify for their third-straight UEFA Champions League appearance, a feat Schalke had never before achieved.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

On 7 October 2014, after a 1–2 defeat to [1899 Hoffenheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSG_1899_Hoffenheim "TSG 1899 Hoffenheim") and after amassing just eight points from seven matches, Keller was sacked and succeeded by [Roberto Di Matteo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Di_Matteo "Roberto Di Matteo").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-newswirengr.com-24)

[![Image 50](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/Domenico_Tedesco.jpg/250px-Domenico_Tedesco.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Domenico_Tedesco.jpg)

[Domenico Tedesco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Tedesco "Domenico Tedesco") was the youngest coach in Schalke's club history.

In the [2014–15 UEFA Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_UEFA_Champions_League "2014–15 UEFA Champions League"), Schalke 04 finished second in a group with Chelsea, [Sporting CP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sporting_CP "Sporting CP") and [Maribor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NK_Maribor "NK Maribor"). Later on, they played against the reigning champion Real Madrid again in the round of 16, where they lost the first leg at home 0–2, but they won 4–3 at the [Santiago Bernabéu Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago_Bernab%C3%A9u_Stadium "Santiago Bernabéu Stadium").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-25) After finishing sixth in the [2014–15 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_Bundesliga "2014–15 Bundesliga"), the club announced the resignation of head coach Roberto Di Matteo on 26 May 2015.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-26) Schalke 04 then played in the Europa League, in the [2015–16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015%E2%80%9316_UEFA_Europa_League "2015–16 UEFA Europa League") and [2016–17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_UEFA_Europa_League "2016–17 UEFA Europa League") seasons, and were eliminated by [Shakhtar Donetsk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Shakhtar_Donetsk "FC Shakhtar Donetsk") and [Ajax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFC_Ajax "AFC Ajax") respectively.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Starting with the [2017–18 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_Bundesliga "2017–18 Bundesliga"), [Domenico Tedesco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Tedesco "Domenico Tedesco") took over the managerial spot for Schalke 04.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-Schalke_beg-27) At the end of the season, he led the team to finish as runners-up to Bayern Munich. On 29 July 2018, the team's captain, [Benedikt Höwedes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedikt_H%C3%B6wedes "Benedikt Höwedes"), decided to leave after more than ten years at the club.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-28)

### 2019–2020: Financial crisis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=FC_Schalke_04&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2019–2020: Financial crisis")]

In the [2018–19 UEFA Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018%E2%80%9319_UEFA_Champions_League "2018–19 UEFA Champions League"), Schalke 04 lost 2–10 on aggregate to [Manchester City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_City_F.C. "Manchester City F.C.") in the round of 16.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-29) Two days later, on 14 March 2019, Tedesco was sacked. [Huub Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huub_Stevens "Huub Stevens") and [Mike Büskens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_B%C3%BCskens "Mike Büskens") took over as [caretaker managers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caretaker_manager "Caretaker manager").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-30) On 9 May 2019, [David Wagner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wagner_(soccer) "David Wagner (soccer)") was appointed as head coach of Schalke 04 on a three-year contract until 30 June 2022.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-31)

Schalke was hit particularly hard by the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), and in April 2020 the club said that it was threatened by bankruptcy.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-tz.de-32) Against the backdrop of a worsened financial situation caused by a high level of debt and a decrease in revenue related to [restrictions put in place to combat the COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_on_association_football#Europe "Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on association football"), the club decided to introduce a player salary cap of €2.5 million per year.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-33)

In the second half of the [2019–20 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%9320_Bundesliga "2019–20 Bundesliga"), Schalke set a new club record of 16 league games without a win between 25 January and 27 June 2020.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-34) Despite this losing streak, Wagner remained as manager,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-35) with [Clemens Tönnies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemens_T%C3%B6nnies "Clemens Tönnies") stepping down from his role as the chairman of Schalke's supervisory board after 19 years in service instead.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-36)

### 2020–present: Relegations and growing financial troubles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=FC_Schalke_04&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2020–present: Relegations and growing financial troubles")]

Schalke started with significant difficulties into the [2020–21 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020%E2%80%9321_Bundesliga "2020–21 Bundesliga"). After 8–0[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-37) and 4–0[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-38) losses away at the hands of Bayern Munich and [RB Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RB_Leipzig "RB Leipzig") and a 1–3[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-39) loss at home against Werder Bremen, Schalke was last in the league table after three games, with one goal scored and fifteen conceded. After only two match days, Schalke dismissed David Wagner as head coach on 27 September in the aftermath of the loss against Bremen.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-40) At 1.08 average points per game, Wagner was then the lowest-scoring head coach in Schalke's recent history.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-41)

Three days later, [Manuel Baum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Baum "Manuel Baum") was nominated as Wagner's successor, with [Naldo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naldo_(footballer,_born_1982) "Naldo (footballer, born 1982)"), a former Schalke player, as assistant coach.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-42) Baum, who had taken over from Wagner at a winless streak of 18 games, was unable to win a single Bundesliga game between the 3rd and 12th match days, and was dismissed ahead of the 13th match day against Arminia Bielefeld.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-:0-43) Huub Stevens once again returned as head coach, beginning his fourth tenure.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-:0-43) Baum's tenure had brought the winless streak up from 18 to 28 Bundesliga games, bringing Schalke to the brink of breaking the all-time record of 31 winless games, set by [SC Tasmania 1900 Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SC_Tasmania_1900_Berlin "SC Tasmania 1900 Berlin") in the [1965–66 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965%E2%80%9366_Bundesliga "1965–66 Bundesliga").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-45) Stevens did not change Schalke's fortunes in his first game, losing the home game against Arminia Bielefeld, themselves in 16th place and thus threatened by relegation, with a 0–1 scoreline.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-46)

On 27 December 2020, Schalke 04 announced that they signed a contract with Swiss manager [Christian Gross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Gross "Christian Gross") to be the head coach of the club until the end of the season, making him the fourth head coach for Schalke 04 during the [2020–21 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020%E2%80%9321_FC_Schalke_04_season "2020–21 FC Schalke 04 season").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-47) Under Gross, Schalke's negative streak continued with a 3–0 loss to [Hertha BSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertha_BSC "Hertha BSC"), marking the 30th consecutive winless game, a losing streak of 358 days.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-49) On 9 January 2021 Schalke finally recorded a victory over [1899 Hoffenheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSG_1899_Hoffenheim "TSG 1899 Hoffenheim"), which meant they avoided matching Tasmania Berlin's record.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-50) It remained Schalke's only victory under Gross, who was sacked as head coach after just eleven matches on 28 February 2021, following losses against rival Borussia Dortmund (0–4) and [VFB Stuttgart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VFB_Stuttgart "VFB Stuttgart") (1–5). Alongside Gross, sporting director Jochen Schneider, team coordinator Sascha Riether, assistant coach Rainer Widmayer and fitness coach Werner Leuthard were also relieved of their duties.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-51) At 0.45 average points per game, Gross was the least successful head coach at Schalke since [Karl-Heinz Marotzke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl-Heinz_Marotzke "Karl-Heinz Marotzke") in 1967.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

On 2 March 2021, [Dimitrios Grammozis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimitrios_Grammozis "Dimitrios Grammozis") was announced as new head coach for Schalke 04.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-Grammozis-52) Grammozis started with a scoreless draw against [Mainz 05](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FSV_Mainz_05 "1. FSV Mainz 05"), but his team was unable to collect any points in the two following matches, which were lost 5–0 against [VfL Wolfsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VfL_Wolfsburg "VfL Wolfsburg") and 3–0 against [Borussia Mönchengladbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borussia_M%C3%B6nchengladbach "Borussia Mönchengladbach"). Schalke did not score a goal in the first three matches under Grammozis, a joined negative record for the club (Helmut Schulte in [1992–93](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992%E2%80%9393_Bundesliga "1992–93 Bundesliga") and Markus Weinzierl in [2016–17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Bundesliga "2016–17 Bundesliga") also waited for the first goal until their fourth match as head coach for Schalke).[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-eurosport_20Mar21-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-54) Against Borussia Mönchengladbach, Schalke conceded its fifth [own goal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Own_goal "Own goal") of the season, yet another negative record.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-eurosport_20Mar21-53)

Relegation to the [2. Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2._Bundesliga "2. Bundesliga") was confirmed on 20 April 2021, as Schalke 04 lost 1–0 to [Arminia Bielefeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arminia_Bielefeld "Arminia Bielefeld"),[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-55) which led to riots by Schalke supporters.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-56)

[![Image 51](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Mike-Bueskens.jpg/250px-Mike-Bueskens.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mike-Bueskens.jpg)

[Mike Büskens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_B%C3%BCskens "Mike Büskens") led Schalke back to the Bundesliga in the [2021–22 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_2._Bundesliga "2021–22 2. Bundesliga").

On 28 February 2022, following [Russia's invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine"), Schalke cancelled their contract with main sponsor [Gazprom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazprom "Gazprom"),[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-57) further straining the club's financial situation. Grammozis was sacked as head coach on 6 March 2022, as promotion back to the [Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundesliga "Bundesliga") appeared uncertain.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-59) He was replaced by Mike Büskens as caretaker manager until the end of the season.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-60) Schalke recovered under Büskens, winning eight of the remaining nine matches. The club secured promotion on 7 May 2022, following a 3–2 victory over [FC St. Pauli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_St._Pauli "FC St. Pauli") that guaranteed a top-two finish in the 2. Bundesliga. Fans invaded the pitch in celebration.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-61) One week later Schalke won the 2. Bundesliga in dramatic fashion[_[tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing\_better\_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles")_] after a 88th-minute winner by [Simon Terodde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Terodde "Simon Terodde") defeating [1. FC Nürnberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_N%C3%BCrnberg "1. FC Nürnberg") 2–1.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-62)

At the end of the [2021–22 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_2._Bundesliga "2021–22 2. Bundesliga"), Büskens moved back to the position of [assistant coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_coach "Assistant coach"). On 7 June 2022, Schalke appointed [Frank Kramer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Kramer_(footballer,_born_1972) "Frank Kramer (footballer, born 1972)") as head coach.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-63) As a result of the club's financial problems, most of the players who were essential for the success in the previous season, like [Ko Itakura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ko_Itakura "Ko Itakura"), could not be kept,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-64) and Schalke struggled to be competitive at the beginning of the [2022–23 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Bundesliga "2022–23 Bundesliga"). Following a series of losses, including a 1–5 against Hoffenheim, Kramer was relieved of his duties on 19 October 2022. At the time, Schalke was 17th in the Bundesliga after ten matchdays.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-66)[Matthias Kreutzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthias_Kreutzer "Matthias Kreutzer") took over as caretaker manager. A week after Kramer's dismissal, on 26 October 2022, sporting director [Rouven Schröder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouven_Schr%C3%B6der "Rouven Schröder") also announced his instant resignation.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-68)

On 27 October 2022, [Thomas Reis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Reis "Thomas Reis") was named as Schalke's new head coach.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-69) The first match under Reis, against [SC Freiburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SC_Freiburg "SC Freiburg"), was lost 0–2, marking Schalke's seventh consecutive loss.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-70) After the game, commentators like [Huub Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huub_Stevens "Huub Stevens") praised the team for its better organization, compared to previous matches.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-71) Schalke finished the first half of the 2022–23 Bundesliga season in 18th and last position in the table, with just nine points to their name.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-73) Following a 1–6 loss against RB Leipzig on match day 17, the club noticeably improved, especially in the defense. Between match days 18 and 21, Schalke played 0–0 four times in a row, a new Bundesliga record.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-74) The following two matches were won, and on 4 March 2023, Schalke left the last place in the table for the first time since October 2022.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-75)

On 19 February 2023, four people were seriously injured when a group of about 100 people, assumed to be supporters of Schalke's rivals [Rot-Weiss Essen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rot-Weiss_Essen "Rot-Weiss Essen") and [Borussia Dortmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borussia_Dortmund "Borussia Dortmund"), attacked a group of Schalke supporters with baseball bats and screwdrivers.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-76) The incident sparked fears over the upcoming derby against Dortmund.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-79) This came less than three weeks after the police had uncovered a possible plot by radical Dortmund supporters, who had tried to hide razor blades behind stickers in the stadium ahead of Dortmund's match against [Mainz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainz_05 "Mainz 05"). In 2014, the police had warned of a similar danger ahead of the derby, after razor blades were found in the stadium hidden behind anti-Schalke stickers.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-80) On 11 March 2023, in the 100th derby between the two clubs, Schalke played 2–2 against Borussia Dortmund, who were in second place at the time.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-81) This ended Dortmund's streak of eight wins in a row.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-82) The police called the match "extremely peaceful", which they attributed to the successful police operation. Media reports noted that several people had been injured by illegal pyrotechnics, with one woman suffering an eye injury. At least one man was taken to the hospital after an intoxicated supporter of the opposing team had bitten off his earlobe.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-83) On the final match-day of the 2022–23 season, Schalke lost 4–2 against RB Leipzig. They finished 17th in the league table, and were relegated again to the 2. Bundesliga.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-84)

After four defeats in the first seven games of the [2023–24 2. Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023%E2%80%9324_2._Bundesliga "2023–24 2. Bundesliga") season, head coach Thomas Reis was sacked on 27 September 2023.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-85) On 8 October 2023, [Karel Geraerts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karel_Geraerts "Karel Geraerts") was appointed as his successor, with a contract until June 2025.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-86) Schalke finished the first half of the season in 14th position, three points ahead of the relegation spots.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-87)

On 3 January 2024, Schalke appointed [Marc Wilmots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Wilmots "Marc Wilmots") as [sporting director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sporting_director "Sporting director"), after sacking [Peter Knäbel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Kn%C3%A4bel "Peter Knäbel").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-89) For Wilmots, who was one of the most prominent former Schalke players,[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-Schalkes_Jahrhundertelf-90) it was his first job as a director.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-91) On 31 January, [Sky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Sports "Sky Sports") reported that Schalke's financial situation may result in the end of the club in its current form by the end of the season. If relegated from the 2. Bundesliga, Schalke would not get a license for the [3. Liga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3._Liga "3. Liga"), and would have to play in the [Regionalliga West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regionalliga_West "Regionalliga West"), the fourth division of German football. In that scenario, the current squad and staff would have to leave the club on a free transfer.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-ran.de_25Feb24-92)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-watson.ch_31Jan24-93) The club formally requested a license for the 3. Liga on 15 March 2024.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-liveticker_18Mar24-94)

The second half of the 2023–24 season started with a series of defeats. The difficult sportive situation was exacerbated by growing unrest within the club, attributed to the relationship between Wilmots, Geraerts, and the team.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-95) After losing 3–0 against [Magdeburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_Magdeburg "1. FC Magdeburg"), Wilmots openly criticized both the squad and head coach Geraerts.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-96) On match-day 24, Schalke achieved a 3–1 surprise victory against league leader [St. Pauli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Pauli "St. Pauli"), which was St. Pauli's first defeat of the season.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-97) Schalke followed up with a strong 3–3 against [SC Paderborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SC_Paderborn "SC Paderborn").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-98) This, together with good individual performances from [Yusuf Kabadayı](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yusuf_Kabaday%C4%B1 "Yusuf Kabadayı") and [Ron Schallenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Schallenberg "Ron Schallenberg"), sparked new hope that the club would be able to avoid relegation.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-99) The following week, after a 5–2 loss against Hertha BSC, Geraerts was criticized heavily again for his lineup, and his lack of tactical direction,[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-101) while Wilmots reaffirmed that Geraerts's position as head coach was not in question.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-liveticker_18Mar24-94)

At the end of 2025, Schalke seemed to have turned things around under new head coach, [Miron Muslić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miron_Musli%C4%87 "Miron Muslić").[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-102) On 2 May 2026, the club clinched promotion to the Bundesliga after finishing first in the [2025–26 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_2._Bundesliga "2025–26 2. Bundesliga"), following a 1–0 win over [Fortuna Düsseldorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortuna_D%C3%BCsseldorf "Fortuna Düsseldorf").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schalke_04#cite_note-103)

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. 12% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts

11% General and Administrative Expenses 
Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[FC Schalke 04](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Schalke_04 "FC Schalke 04") is a German [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football")[club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_football_clubs_in_Germany "List of football clubs in Germany") based in [Gelsenkirchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelsenkirchen "Gelsenkirchen"), [North Rhine-Westphalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Rhine-Westphalia "North Rhine-Westphalia").

Where your donation goes

 Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](https://wikimediafoundation.org/annualreports/current/) for more information about our financial health. 

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

12% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 
Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

11% General and Administrative Expenses 
Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[FC Schalke 04](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Schalke_04 "FC Schalke 04") is a German [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football")[club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_football_clubs_in_Germany "List of football clubs in Germany") based in [Gelsenkirchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelsenkirchen "Gelsenkirchen"), [North Rhine-Westphalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Rhine-Westphalia "North Rhine-Westphalia").

The **[2022–23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_in_German_football "2022–23 in German football")[FC Schalke 04](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Schalke_04 "FC Schalke 04") season** was the 119th season in the [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") club's history and [first consecutive and 54th overall season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_clubs_in_the_Bundesliga "List of clubs in the Bundesliga") in the topflight of [German football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_football_league_system "German football league system"), the [Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundesliga "Bundesliga"), having been promoted from the [2. Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2._Bundesliga "2. Bundesliga") in [2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_2._Bundesliga "2021–22 2. Bundesliga"). In addition to the domestic league, Schalke also participated in this season's edition of the [domestic cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_in_Germany#German_Cup "Football in Germany"), the [DFB-Pokal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DFB-Pokal "DFB-Pokal"). This was the 22nd season for Schalke in the [Veltins-Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_AufSchalke "Arena AufSchalke"), located in [Gelsenkirchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelsenkirchen "Gelsenkirchen"), [North Rhine-Westphalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Rhine-Westphalia "North Rhine-Westphalia"). The season covers a period from 1 July 2022 to 30 June 2023. Schalke were relegated on the final matchday of the season.

## Season summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Season summary")]

On 7 June 2022, Schalke appointed [Frank Kramer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Kramer_(footballer,_born_1972) "Frank Kramer (footballer, born 1972)") as head coach.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-1) As a result of the club's financial problems, most of the players who were essential for the success in the previous season, like [Ko Itakura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ko_Itakura "Ko Itakura"), could not be kept,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-2) and Schalke struggled to be competitive at the beginning of the [2022–23 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Bundesliga "2022–23 Bundesliga"). Following a series of losses, including a 1–5 against Hoffenheim, Kramer was relieved of his duties on 19 October 2022. At the time, Schalke was 17th in the Bundesliga after ten matchdays.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-4)[Matthias Kreutzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthias_Kreutzer "Matthias Kreutzer") took over as caretaker manager. A week after Kramer's dismissal, on 26 October 2022, sporting director [Rouven Schröder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouven_Schr%C3%B6der "Rouven Schröder") also announced his instant resignation.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-6)

On 27 October 2022, [Thomas Reis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Reis "Thomas Reis") was named as Schalke's new head coach.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-7) The first match under Reis, against [SC Freiburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SC_Freiburg "SC Freiburg"), was lost 0–2, marking Schalke's seventh consecutive loss.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-8) After the game, commentators like [Huub Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huub_Stevens "Huub Stevens") praised the team for its better organization, compared to previous matches.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-9) Schalke finished the first half of the 2022–23 Bundesliga season in 18th and last position in the table, with just nine points to their name.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-11) Following a 1–6 loss against RB Leipzig on match day 17, the club noticeably improved, especially in the defense. Between match days 18 and 21, Schalke played 0–0 four times in a row, a new Bundesliga record.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-12) The following two matches were won, and on 4 March 2023, Schalke left the last place in the table for the first time since October 2022.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-13)

On 19 February 2023, four people were seriously injured when a group of about 100 people, assumed to be supporters of Schalke's rivals [Rot-Weiss Essen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rot-Weiss_Essen "Rot-Weiss Essen") and [Borussia Dortmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borussia_Dortmund "Borussia Dortmund"), attacked a group of Schalke supporters with baseball bats and screwdrivers.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-14) The incident sparked fears over the upcoming derby against Dortmund.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-17) This came less than three weeks after the police had uncovered a possible plot by radical Dortmund supporters, who had tried to hide razor blades behind stickers in the stadium ahead of Dortmund's match against [Mainz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainz_05 "Mainz 05"). In 2014, the police had warned of a similar danger ahead of the derby, after razor blades were found in the stadium hidden behind anti-Schalke stickers.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-18) On 11 March 2023, in the 100th derby between the two clubs, Schalke played 2–2 against Borussia Dortmund, who were in second place at the time.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-19) This ended Dortmund's streak of eight wins in a row.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-20) The police called the match "extremely peaceful", which they attributed to the successful police operation. Media reports noted that several people had been injured by illegal pyrotechnics, with one woman suffering an eye injury. At least one man was taken to the hospital after an intoxicated supporter of the opposing team had bitten off his earlobe.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_FC_Schalke_04_season#cite_note-21) On the final match-day of the 2022–23 season, Schalke lost 4–2 against RB Leipzig. They finished 17th in the league table, and were relegated again to the 2. Bundesliga.
