**Spielvereinigung Greuther Fürth** (German pronunciation:[[ˈʃpiːlfɛɐ̯ˌʔaɪnɪɡʊŋ ˌɡʁɔɪ̯tɐ ˈfʏʁt]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Standard_German "Help:IPA/Standard German")), commonly known as **Greuther Fürth** (German pronunciation:[[ˌɡʁɔɪ̯tɐ ˈfʏʁt]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Standard_German "Help:IPA/Standard German")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/b/bc/De-Greuther_F%C3%BCrth.ogg/De-Greuther_F%C3%BCrth.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:De-Greuther_F%C3%BCrth.ogg "File:De-Greuther Fürth.ogg")) or by their historical name, **SpVgg Fürth**, is a [German football club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_in_Germany "Football in Germany") based in [Fürth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%BCrth "Fürth"), [Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria "Bavaria"). They play in the [2. Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2._Bundesliga "2. Bundesliga"), the second tier of the [German football league system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_football_league_system "German football league system"), following relegation from the [Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundesliga "Bundesliga") in the [2021–22 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Bundesliga "2021–22 Bundesliga").

Founded in 1903, the most successful era for Greuther Fürth came in the pre-Bundesliga era in the 1910s and 1920s, when the club won three [German championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_German_football_champions "List of German football champions"), in [1914](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1914_German_football_championship "1914 German football championship"), [1926](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1926_German_football_championship "1926 German football championship"), and [1929](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1929_German_football_championship "1929 German football championship") respectively, and finished as runners-up in [1920](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1920_German_football_championship "1920 German football championship"). In the [2012–13 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Bundesliga "2012–13 Bundesliga"), the club played in the Bundesliga for the first time, having won promotion from the 2. Bundesliga;[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-2) they were relegated back to the 2. Bundesliga at the end of the season. On 23 May 2021, they[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] were promoted back to the Bundesliga for the second time.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-3) Upon placing 18th in the Bundesliga table in the 2021–22 season, they were relegated back to 2. Bundesliga.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Spielvereinigung Fürth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Spielvereinigung Fürth")]

[![Image 32: Wikimedia Commons logo](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/4a/Commons-logo.svg/40px-Commons-logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Commons-logo.svg)

Wikimedia Commons has media related to [SpVgg Greuther Fürth kits](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/SpVgg%20Greuther%20F%C3%BCrth%20kits "commons:SpVgg Greuther Fürth kits").

The origins of _SpVgg Fürth_ are in the establishment on 23 September 1903 of a football department within the gymnastics club _[Turnverein 1860 Fürth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV\_1860\_F%C3%BCrth "TV 1860 Fürth")_. The footballers went their own way as an independent club in November 1906, after they did not get enough support from _TV Fürth_. The team played in the Ostkreisliga and took divisional titles there in 1912, 1913 and 1914 before moving on to participate in the Süddeutsche (South German) regional playoffs for the national championship round.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-Gr%C3%BCne,_Hardy_2001-4) Right from the beginning, there was a great rivalry between the SpVgg Fürth and the [1. FC Nürnberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_N%C3%BCrnberg "1. FC Nürnberg"), predicated on the historical rivalry between the two neighbouring cities.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-5) The club grew rapidly, and by 1914, it had 3,000 members and was the largest sports club in Germany.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] When the club built their own stadium, [Sportpark Ronhof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer "Sportpark Ronhof Thomas Sommer"), in 1910, it was the biggest stadium in Germany at the time.

#### National champions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: National champions")]

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Greuther_Feurth_-_Historische_Logos.png/250px-Greuther_Feurth_-_Historische_Logos.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Greuther_Feurth_-_Historische_Logos.png)

Historical logos of Greuther Fürth

Fürth won their first national title, the [1914 German football championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1914_German_football_championship "1914 German football championship"), under English coach [William Townley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Townley "William Townley") with [left winger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midfielder#Winger "Midfielder")[Julius Hirsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Hirsch "Julius Hirsch"), who had joined the team the prior season.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-auto-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-7) They faced [VfB Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VfB_Leipzig "VfB Leipzig")– the defending champions with three titles to their credit– in the final held on 31 May in [Magdeburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdeburg "Magdeburg"). A 154-minute-long thriller,[_[tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing\_better\_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles")_] the longest completed game in German football history (the 1922 Final was abandoned after 189 minutes due to darkness), ended with Fürth scoring a [golden goal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_goal "Golden goal") to secure the title.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-8)

The team had a solid[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] run of successes through the 1920s and into the early 1930s, beginning with an appearance in the national final in 1920 against 1. FC Nürnberg, which was the dominant side of the decade.[_[according to whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] The rivalry between the two clubs was such that a star[_[tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing\_better\_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles")_] player with SpVgg was forced to leave after he married a woman from the city of [Nuremberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg "Nuremberg").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In 1924, for the first and only time, the Germany national side was made up exclusively of players from just two sides– Fürth and 1. FC Nürnberg– and players of the two teams slept in separate rail coaches.

SpVgg showed regularly on the national stage,[_[tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing\_better\_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles")_] advancing to the semi-finals in 1923 and 1931. They claimed two more championships– in 1926 and 1929– with both of those victories coming at the expense of [Hertha BSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertha_BSC "Hertha BSC"). Through this period, the club played five finals in the Süddeutscher Pokal (en:South German Cup), coming away as cup winners on four occasions. On 27 August 1929, the association was joined by _FC Schneidig Fürth_.

German football was re-organized in 1933 under the [Third Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Reich "Third Reich") into 16 top flight [Gauligen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauliga "Gauliga"). Fürth became part of the [Gauliga Bayern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauliga_Bayern "Gauliga Bayern"), but their success over the next dozen[_[quantify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] seasons was limited to a division title there in 1935, alongside regular appearances in competition for the Tschammerpokal, predecessor to today's [DFB-Pokal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DFB-Pokal "DFB-Pokal") (German Cup).

#### Postwar play

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Postwar play")]

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Greuther_Furth_Performance_Chart.png/330px-Greuther_Furth_Performance_Chart.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Greuther_Furth_Performance_Chart.png)

Historical chart of Greuther Fürth and predecessors' performance

After the war, the team struggled through three seasons in the [Oberliga Süd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberliga_S%C3%BCd_(1945%E2%80%9363) "Oberliga Süd (1945–63)") (I) before slipping to the [Landesliga Bayern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landesliga_Bayern "Landesliga Bayern") (II).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]_SpVgg_ quickly recovered itself and returned to Oberliga play the next season. They[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] won the title there in 1950 and went on to the national playoffs, advancing as far as the semi-finals before being eliminated 1–4 by [VfB Stuttgart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VfB_Stuttgart "VfB Stuttgart").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In 1954, two players from the _SpVgg_, [Karl Mai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Mai "Karl Mai") and [Herbert Erhardt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Erhardt "Herbert Erhardt"), were members of the "[Miracle of Bern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miracle_of_Bern "Miracle of Bern")" team that won Germany's first [World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1954_FIFA_World_Cup "1954 FIFA World Cup").

Fürth remained a first division side until the formation of the Bundesliga in 1963. The club did not qualify as one of the sixteen teams that made up the new unified national first division and they found themselves playing second division football in the [Regionalliga Süd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regionalliga_S%C3%BCd_(1963%E2%80%9374) "Regionalliga Süd (1963–74)"), where they were generally a mid-table side whose best finish was third-place result in 1967.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The club played in the [2. Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2._Bundesliga "2. Bundesliga") from its inception in 1974 until 1983 with their best performance a fourth-place result in 1978–79.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] They slipped to playing in the tier III [Bayernliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayernliga "Bayernliga"), with a short three-year spell in the fourth division [Landesliga Bayern-Mitte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landesliga_Bayern-Mitte "Landesliga Bayern-Mitte") in the late 1980s.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] At this time, the club started to have large financial problems.[_[why?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_][_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] In 1990, Fürth celebrated a 3–1 victory in the opening round of the DFB-Pokal play [over first division side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Bundesliga_clubs_eliminated_from_the_DFB-Pokal_by_amateur_sides "List of Bundesliga clubs eliminated from the DFB-Pokal by amateur sides")[Borussia Dortmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borussia_Dortmund "Borussia Dortmund") before going out 0–1 to [1. FC Saarbrücken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_Saarbr%C3%BCcken "1. FC Saarbrücken") in the second round.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] They returned to the Bayernliga (III) in 1991 and the Regionalliga Süd (III) in 1994.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] But still, the club's financial issues became bigger,[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] and they were forced to sell their ground to the local businessman [Conny Brandstätter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conny_Brandst%C3%A4tter?action=edit&redlink=1 "Conny Brandstätter (page does not exist)").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] As the financial problems continued to grow,[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] the president of _SpVgg_, Edgar Burkhart, arranged a deal with Helmut Hack, president of [TSV Vestenbergsgreuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSV_Vestenbergsgreuth "TSV Vestenbergsgreuth"), to let _TSV_ join the _SpVgg_ and changing the name of the _Spielvereinigung_ to the name _SpVgg Greuther Fürth_, which is still in use.[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_][_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The _SpVgg_ so had the chance to get back in both financial and on-pitch success,[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] while _TSV_ could grow bigger in the city of Fürth than it would have been possible in the village of [Vestenbergsgreuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestenbergsgreuth "Vestenbergsgreuth").

### TSV Vestenbergsgreuth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: TSV Vestenbergsgreuth")]

Main article: [TSV Vestenbergsgreuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSV_Vestenbergsgreuth "TSV Vestenbergsgreuth")

Meanwhile, the small village team of _TSV Vestenbergsgreuth_ was established 1 February 1974 and debuted as a fourth division side.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-Gr%C3%BCne,_Hardy_2001-4) They advanced into the Amateur Oberliga Bayern (III) in 1987, just as SpVgg Fürth was descending to play in the division the more junior club had just escaped. _TSV_ took part in the national amateur playoff round in 1988 and 1995. Their best performance came in the 1995 DFB-Pokal when they upset [Bayern Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayern_Munich "Bayern Munich") 1–0, and then beat [FC 08 Homburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_08_Homburg "FC 08 Homburg") 5–1, before being eliminated in the third round of the competition by [VfL Wolfsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VfL_Wolfsburg "VfL Wolfsburg") on penalty kicks.

### SpVgg Greuther Fürth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: SpVgg Greuther Fürth")]

At the time when Vestenbergsgreuth's football branch was incorporated in 1996, in which TSV's football players came over to Fürth, both clubs were playing at about the same level in Regionalliga Süd (III). The SpVgg was runner-up behind long-term rival 1. FC Nürnberg in the division the next year, and so earned promotion back to the 2. Bundesliga after 18 years, and played in the second tier at the first time since 1979. At this time, the _Sportpark Ronhof_, now called _Playmobil Arena_, faced the first major redevelopment since the post-war years and the construction of the old main stand in 1950. They built new stands on three of the four sides of the pitch, a roofed seating stand on the opposite side of the main stand, an uncovered terrace in the north end, and an uncovered mixed standing and seating area in the south of the stadium, as well as installing [floodlights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floodlights "Floodlights") in the _Ronhof_ the first time ever.[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] With the modernized stadium and a clever[_[according to whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] transfer strategy, they have consistently finished in the top half of the 18-team table in the 2000s,[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] despite having one of the lowest budgets most of the time.[_[according to whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] On 1 July 2003, the club added former workers' club _[Tuspo Fürth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuspo\_F%C3%BCrth "Tuspo Fürth")_ to its tradition through a merger. In 2008, the stadium faced another redevelopment, as the standing terrace in the north got a roof, and a VIP building was installed near to the old main stand. With this work, the main stand became the last piece of the stadium that has not been redeveloped.[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] In that time, Fürth has come close[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] to renewing its ancient rivalry with Nürnberg at the Bundesliga level, narrowly missing promotion in each of the first two seasons of the 2010s. On 23 April 2012, Fürth finally gained promotion to the Bundesliga in the [2011–12 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011%E2%80%9312_2._Bundesliga "2011–12 2. Bundesliga"), eventually winning the [2. Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2._Bundesliga "2. Bundesliga") under manager [Mike Büskens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_B%C3%BCskens "Mike Büskens"). With promotion, the 1998-built south stand was demolished, and a new one was installed, gaining a capacity increase from 14,500 to 18,000, as well as providing a roof on the south for the first time.

However, Fürth had a difficult first season in the Bundesliga as the club amassed only four victories in the 34-game campaign, one of them at the ground of their rivals 1. FC Nürnberg, when the de facto relegated side won 1–0, giving the fans of the _Kleeblatt_ a peaceful feeling about the relegation.[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] The club also set an infamous[_[according to whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] record by becoming the first club in Bundesliga history to not win a single home game during the regular season.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-9) The club finished last in the league with 21 points and was relegated back to the 2. Bundesliga.

The following season, despite not aiming for promotion, the club was a strong contender for a direct return to the Bundesliga.[_[according to whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] A third place in the final standings qualified the team for the promotion play-offs, where it faced [Hamburger SV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburger_SV "Hamburger SV"). After a 0–0 draw in [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"), the club missed out on promotion on the away goal rule when the return leg ended 1–1. In the following seasons, they struggled to be as strong as they were before the Bundesliga promotion. They nearly got relegated to the [3. Liga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3._Liga "3. Liga") in the [2014–15 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_2._Bundesliga "2014–15 2. Bundesliga"), when only a narrow win against later promoted club [SV Darmstadt 98](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SV_Darmstadt_98 "SV Darmstadt 98") on matchday 33, and other teams not winning on matchday 34, kept them in the league. In the same season, on early matchday 2, they gained a historic[_[tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing\_better\_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles")_] 5–1 home victory in the [Frankenderby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankenderby "Frankenderby"), their highest-ever home win in a derby. In the following two years, the _Spielvereinigung_ finished mid-table, with not having either fear of getting relegated or gaining promotion. This period of their newer history is characterized by the relegation of _FCN_ in 2014, and both rivals playing each year since then. In the [2016–17 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_2._Bundesliga "2016–17 2. Bundesliga"), the _Kleeblatt_ won both derbies of the regular season for the first time since the 1970s, and finished above Nuremberg for the first time since the 1950s. In early 2016, the 1950-built main stand was demolished, and the construction of a new main stand started. Before the [2017–18 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_2._Bundesliga "2017–18 2. Bundesliga"), the construction of the new main stand was finished. With a 3–1 victory over [Fortuna Düsseldorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortuna_D%C3%BCsseldorf "Fortuna Düsseldorf") on 17 September 2017, the club became leader of the all-time league table of the 2. Bundesliga.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-10)

By finishing second in the [2020–21 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020%E2%80%9321_2._Bundesliga "2020–21 2. Bundesliga"), Greuther Fürth gained promotion to the Bundesliga for the second time in the club's history. Under manager [Stefan Leitl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefan_Leitl "Stefan Leitl"), the team secured promotion on the last matchday of the season with a 3–2 victory over Fortuna Düsseldorf.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-11)

## Rivals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Rivals")]

Main article: [Bavarian football derbies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_football_derbies "Bavarian football derbies")

[1. FC Nürnberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_N%C3%BCrnberg "1. FC Nürnberg") is by far Fürth’s biggest rival, going back to the early days of German football when, at times, those two clubs dominated the national championship.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-12) In German, matches between the two sides are known as the "Frankenderby”.

Nürnberg are the most recent winners in this rivalry, having beat Fürth 4-2 away in the 2. Bundesliga in August 2026. [[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-13)

Their minor rivals also include [Bayern Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayern_Munich "Bayern Munich").

### Notable fans

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Notable fans")]

In September 2012, former [United States Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State")[Henry Kissinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kissinger "Henry Kissinger"), whose family fled Nazi Germany in 1938, attended a SpVgg match against [Schalke 04](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Schalke_04 "FC Schalke 04"). He had promised to attend a game at the Ronhof stadium if the team were promoted to the top-flight Bundesliga. As a child, Kissinger had tried to watch games there, despite it being against his parents' wishes.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpVgg_Greuther_F%C3%BCrth#cite_note-20) Kissinger was an honorary member of SpVgg, and for decades he kept himself informed about match results and held contact to the club.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] During his time serving in the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") in the 1970s, he reportedly asked his staff to have the team's weekend result ready for him on Monday mornings.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] He visited his hometown and the club several times and attended a Bundesliga match in 2012 during the team's first season in the Bundesliga.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

**Sportpark Ronhof | Thomas Sommer**[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-Juli2014-2) is an [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football")[stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium "Stadium") in the district of [Ronhof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronhof?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ronhof (page does not exist)") in [Fürth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%BCrth "Fürth"), [Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria "Bavaria"), Germany, and the home ground of [2 Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2_Bundesliga "2 Bundesliga") team SpVgg Greuther Fürth.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-Stadion-3)

The stadium was originally opened on 11 September 1910 under the name _**Sportplatz am Ronhofer Weg gegenüber dem Zentral-Friedhof**_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-Stadion-3) (English: Sports ground on Ronhof Lane opposite the central cemetery). It was expanded several times (max. 28,000 capacity) but later reduced to 15,500 and today holds a capacity crowd of 16,626.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-Stadion-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Early history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early history")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/1910match.jpg/250px-1910match.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1910match.jpg)

SpVgg Greuther Fürth match in 1910

On September 11, 1910, the stadium was inaugurated on the territory of the then still independent municipality of Ronhof. A small wooden grandstand, as well as standing walls, provided space for about 8000 people. SpVgg (Greuther) Fürth is thus one of the German football clubs that have been playing on their current pitch for the longest time.

Just one year later, the grandstand was enlarged and provided with changing rooms and showers. This meant that 10,000 spectators could now watch the games. In 1919, the stadium was enlarged again- higher earthen walls and wider standing-room steps now provided space for 25,000 people.

In April 1945, the grandstand was hit during an air raid and burned out. An unroofed makeshift stand did its work until May 20, 1951, when the new main stand was inaugurated. It stood with few external changes until its demolition in 2016.

The stadium had a record attendance shortly before this inauguration: on April 1, 30,000 spectators came to the [derby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankenderby "Frankenderby") against [1. FC Nürnberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_N%C3%BCrnberg "1. FC Nürnberg"), causing the barrier to the pitch to collapse. Nevertheless, everything remained peaceful and the match ended 1–0. This record was set again on April 3, 1952, when 32,000 spectators filled the stadium, also against 1. FC Nürnberg.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-:0-4) The match ended 3:3.

### Financial problems

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Financial problems")]

In 1983, due to the oppressive debt burden of SpVgg, the Sportpark Ronhof was sold to [Horst Brandstätter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horst_Brandst%C3%A4tter "Horst Brandstätter") ([Playmobil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playmobil "Playmobil")).

In 1996, the football department of [TSV Vestenbergsgreuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSV_Vestenbergsgreuth "TSV Vestenbergsgreuth") joined the _SpVgg Fürth 1903_ and the club name was changed to _SpVgg Greuther Fürth_. The stadium of SpVgg Fürth - the Ronhof - was chosen as the venue. With the promotion to the [2. Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2._Fu%C3%9Fball-Bundesliga "2. Fußball-Bundesliga") in 1997, the stadium had to meet new requirements. Previously, there had been no block divisions, no floodlights, an analog scoreboard, and no separation of visiting fans. After both Horst Brandstätter and the city of Fürth were convinced of the importance of the conversion measures, the undertaking could begin.

### Modernization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Modernization")]

On July 19, 1997, the new _Playmobil Stadium_ was inaugurated with a match against TSV 1860 Munich. The home side won 1–0, with the capacity dropping from around 2,500 seated and 24,500 standing to 5,000 seated and 9,500 standing. The main stand (2,500 seats), as well as the south stand (4,300 standing) and _Block and 1_ (700 standing), remained in their previous form- however, fences were erected to separate the fan groups. The north stand (4,500 standing room) was built with prefabricated concrete elements - the back straight (3,000 seats) consists of a tubular steel stand with plastic seats and a Teflon roof. A video screen was also installed, the entrance area was redesigned and new ticket offices were built.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Tag_BTSV-Spiel_Danach.jpg/250px-Tag_BTSV-Spiel_Danach.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tag_BTSV-Spiel_Danach.jpg)

Inside the Stadium after a game against Braunschweig in 2023

In July 1999, the south stand was leveled and a tubular steel structure was erected for seating and standing room. When it was completed in August, the new floodlights were inaugurated. The standing room in the south stand can accommodate about 1,200 guests, while the seating capacity is 4,500.

In August 2003, the stadium received a new video wall. Three years later, this was renewed again. The current scoreboard measures 9.23 by 6.78 meters.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-5)

During the 2007 summer break, a turf heating system was installed, new seats for the main stand were installed, and the old Block 1 was demolished. In the summer of 2008, the standing terraces of the north stand were roofed over. In addition, the corners between the counter stand and the adjoining blocks were closed off with media walls. A modular VIP building for 700 spectators was erected on the site of the former Block 1.

Since 2010, the entire stadium has been fitted with seats in the club colors of white and green, and the back straight bears the lettering _Kleeblatt_. The former main stand was given a new coat of paint. In 2011, the formerly colorful floodlights were painted white-green and fans redesigned the breakwaters and the entrance area of the north stand.

### Abandoned new stadium plans

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Abandoned new stadium plans")]

After interim plans to build a new stadium on the [Main-Danube Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main-Danube_Canal "Main-Danube Canal") in the south of the city, SpVgg Greuther Fürth extended its lease with the owner until 2040 in November 2012.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-6)

### Redevelopment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Redevelopment")]

In August 2015, the lease was extended another time, currently until 2050.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-7) At the same time, a decision was made to rebuild the main grandstand. The reconstruction took place in two phases: Phase 1, which included the demolition of the now 60-year-old main grandstand and a subsequent new construction with VIP stands, started in January 2016 and was completed by July 2017. To this end, the infrastructure around the stadium was also expanded away from the conversion of the grandstand. The previous training pitches behind the stadium were replaced by car parking spaces, for which a circular road was also drawn around the stadium. During the new construction, makeshift containers were used for changing rooms and media rooms, which were set up behind the back straight. Players entered the stadium through the open corner between the north stand and the back straight. In the second construction phase, which should have lasted until December 2017 but was delayed by several changes of architect and was not completed until the start of the 2017/18 season, the interior of the new main stand was fitted out. This provided the latter with meeting and conference rooms in addition to the infrastructure for the football events. These replaced the previous VIP North building, which had already been dismantled and sold. In its place, the main stand was extended to the north. The gap to the North Stand was closed before the 2018/19 season.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-8) It is still planned to extend the main stand to the south, which should thereby replace blocks A and B.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-9)

## Structure and facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Structure and facilities")]

After SpVgg Greuther Fürth's promotion to the Bundesliga in 2012, the south stand was rebuilt, increasing the stadium's capacity by 3,000 seats to 18,000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-10)

The south stand, where the away section is located, was completely roofed over.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-11) With the completion of the new main stand, the capacity decreased to 16,626 seats, as tickets are no longer sold in the adjacent blocks A and B in the south for reasons of visual obstruction. In total, there is room for 8,500 standing fans, slightly more than seats (8,126). The stadium is 100% covered.The capacity is divided as follows:

### Main stand

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Main stand")]

The main stand of the Ronhof is the heart of the stadium. After the old stand from 1951, as well as a temporal stand in front of it, were demolished, the club built a new grandstand with a revamped and vastly expanded VIP section, a new players' and match officials' area and a dedicated press space. Its internal area is used throughout the year for corporate events, as the different areas of the stand can be rented. The new stand has the same breadth as the old main stand. After its completion in 2017, the old VIP building to the north was demolished and a public grandstand in the same style as the new main stand was built, seating about 1,100 people and also functions as the home of the new club shop. Completed in summer 2018, the combined, completely covered, structure seats just under 2,700 spectators.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-12)

### North Stand

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: North Stand")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/2012-11-11_Fuerth2_%288208563665%29.jpg/250px-2012-11-11_Fuerth2_%288208563665%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2012-11-11_Fuerth2_(8208563665).jpg)

The North Stand

The North Stand is built as a terrace, and is home to the most vocal Fans of the "Kleeblatt". It was built in 1997 as a standing-room-only stand on the ground of the old, curved and which still functions as foundation to the stand. In 2008, the terrace along with the vestibule of the stand were covered with a roof, making it weatherproof. The north stand has room for 4,200 people in three sections, with Fürth's ultra groups finding their home in Block 3. Between the renovation 2008 and 2025, this section was split up to form a supporter-dedicated "Block 12", but due to the wish of the fans and the growth of their groups, this change has been reversed prior to the 2025/2026 season.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-13)

### Back straight

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Back straight")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Fuerth_Arena_Gegentribuene_2012-12-01.jpg/250px-Fuerth_Arena_Gegentribuene_2012-12-01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fuerth_Arena_Gegentribuene_2012-12-01.jpg)

The back straight in 2011.

Also built in 1997 to replace the old back straight with its legendary poplars, which fell victim to the reconstruction. It is a seating-only stand, seats approximately 3,000 people, and is the lowest stand in the stadium. Since 2018, there has been a beer garden behind it. In addition, the family block was moved from the south stand to the area of the back straight adjacent to the north stand.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-14)

### South End

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: South End")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Tag_HSV-Spiel.jpg/250px-Tag_HSV-Spiel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tag_HSV-Spiel.jpg)

View to the new South Stand, built in 2012

The new Südkurve (or south end) was also built after the promotion in 2012 in place of the old Südtribüne. In the process, the new stand was completely covered and provided with its own floodlights, since the roof restricts the light field of the floodlights. In front of blocks, A and B is a raised and covered platform with a ramp for wheelchair users. The only built-up curve in the stadium is occupied by the "Der Lohner" standing stand, which is named after the late former club president [Edgar Burkart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Burkart?action=edit&redlink=1 "Edgar Burkart (page does not exist)"), known as Lohner. Behind the goal, there is a seating grandstand, which is built somewhat lower in the area of the scoreboard. Adjacent to this is the away section, whose standing-room area has been carried over without change from the times before promotion. In total, the south stand can accommodate around 8,300 people. However, due to the new main stand being built approximately five meters closer to the pitch than before, the capacity of the south stand is restricted to about 6,700 people, as the sectors A and B as well as a part of the standing sector have no line of sight to the northern half of the pitch and are closed.

### Corners

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Corners")]

The corners of the stadium, with the exception of the southern corner on the side of the main stand, are currently not covered with stands. While there are two large advertising boards and the floodlight masts on the side of the back straight, there is a view from the entrance area of the North Stand between the North and Main Stands on the northern side of the Main Stand. There is also a floodlight mast here. There is also a passageway between the main stand and the south curve, so that it is theoretically possible to see a few square meters of the pitch from the street without a ticket.

## Name sponsorship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Name sponsorship")]

From 1997 to 2010, the Ronhof was officially called _Playmobil Stadium_. At that time, [Horst Brandstätter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horst_Brandst%C3%A4tter "Horst Brandstätter"), inventor and owner of [Playmobil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playmobil "Playmobil"), owned the stadium.

At the start of the 2010–11 season, [Mederer Süßwarenvertriebs GmbH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trolli "Trolli") (now Trolli GmbH) bought the naming rights to the stadium. Between July 2010 and June 2014, the stadium was thus called _Trolli Arena_.

From the expiration of the sponsorship agreement on July 1, 2014, until February 1, 2016, the _Ronhof_ temporarily bore the official name _Stadion am Laubenweg_.

In February 2016, it was renamed _Sportpark Ronhof | Thomas Sommer_. The new name is composed of the traditional name of the stadium and that of the Fürth-born real estate dealer _Thomas Sommer_, who became [Name Sponsor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sponsor_(commercial) "Sponsor (commercial)") until the summer of 2021.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-sportparkSommer-15) In August 2019, Sommer confirmed the extension of the sponsorship contract beyond 2021 and this regardless of the league. Per year, the contract brings SpVgg half a million euros.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-16) In November 2019, it was announced that the sponsorship agreement had been extended into 2025.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-17)

## Other uses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Other uses")]

The [Germany women's national football team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_women's_national_football_team "Germany women's national football team") has used the stadium for three international matches. The matches took place on September 23, 1999, against [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine_women's_national_football_team "Ukraine women's national football team"), on March 4, 2004, against [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_women's_national_football_team "China women's national football team"), and on April 8, 2015, against [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_women's_national_football_team "Brazil women's national football team").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-18)

**Sportpark Ronhof | Thomas Sommer**[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-Juli2014-2) is an [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football")[stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium "Stadium") in the district of [Ronhof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronhof?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ronhof (page does not exist)") in [Fürth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%BCrth "Fürth"), [Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria "Bavaria"), Germany, and the home ground of [2 Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2_Bundesliga "2 Bundesliga") team SpVgg Greuther Fürth.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-Stadion-3)

The stadium was originally opened on 11 September 1910 under the name _**Sportplatz am Ronhofer Weg gegenüber dem Zentral-Friedhof**_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-Stadion-3) (English: Sports ground on Ronhof Lane opposite the central cemetery). It was expanded several times (max. 28,000 capacity) but later reduced to 15,500 and today holds a capacity crowd of 16,626.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-Stadion-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Early history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early history")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/1910match.jpg/250px-1910match.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1910match.jpg)

SpVgg Greuther Fürth match in 1910

On September 11, 1910, the stadium was inaugurated on the territory of the then still independent municipality of Ronhof. A small wooden grandstand, as well as standing walls, provided space for about 8000 people. SpVgg (Greuther) Fürth is thus one of the German football clubs that have been playing on their current pitch for the longest time.

Just one year later, the grandstand was enlarged and provided with changing rooms and showers. This meant that 10,000 spectators could now watch the games. In 1919, the stadium was enlarged again- higher earthen walls and wider standing-room steps now provided space for 25,000 people.

In April 1945, the grandstand was hit during an air raid and burned out. An unroofed makeshift stand did its work until May 20, 1951, when the new main stand was inaugurated. It stood with few external changes until its demolition in 2016.

The stadium had a record attendance shortly before this inauguration: on April 1, 30,000 spectators came to the [derby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankenderby "Frankenderby") against [1. FC Nürnberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_N%C3%BCrnberg "1. FC Nürnberg"), causing the barrier to the pitch to collapse. Nevertheless, everything remained peaceful and the match ended 1–0. This record was set again on April 3, 1952, when 32,000 spectators filled the stadium, also against 1. FC Nürnberg.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-:0-4) The match ended 3:3.

### Financial problems

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Financial problems")]

In 1983, due to the oppressive debt burden of SpVgg, the Sportpark Ronhof was sold to [Horst Brandstätter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horst_Brandst%C3%A4tter "Horst Brandstätter") ([Playmobil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playmobil "Playmobil")).

In 1996, the football department of [TSV Vestenbergsgreuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSV_Vestenbergsgreuth "TSV Vestenbergsgreuth") joined the _SpVgg Fürth 1903_ and the club name was changed to _SpVgg Greuther Fürth_. The stadium of SpVgg Fürth - the Ronhof - was chosen as the venue. With the promotion to the [2. Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2._Fu%C3%9Fball-Bundesliga "2. Fußball-Bundesliga") in 1997, the stadium had to meet new requirements. Previously, there had been no block divisions, no floodlights, an analog scoreboard, and no separation of visiting fans. After both Horst Brandstätter and the city of Fürth were convinced of the importance of the conversion measures, the undertaking could begin.

### Modernization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Modernization")]

On July 19, 1997, the new _Playmobil Stadium_ was inaugurated with a match against TSV 1860 Munich. The home side won 1–0, with the capacity dropping from around 2,500 seated and 24,500 standing to 5,000 seated and 9,500 standing. The main stand (2,500 seats), as well as the south stand (4,300 standing) and _Block and 1_ (700 standing), remained in their previous form- however, fences were erected to separate the fan groups. The north stand (4,500 standing room) was built with prefabricated concrete elements - the back straight (3,000 seats) consists of a tubular steel stand with plastic seats and a Teflon roof. A video screen was also installed, the entrance area was redesigned and new ticket offices were built.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Tag_BTSV-Spiel_Danach.jpg/250px-Tag_BTSV-Spiel_Danach.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tag_BTSV-Spiel_Danach.jpg)

Inside the Stadium after a game against Braunschweig in 2023

In July 1999, the south stand was leveled and a tubular steel structure was erected for seating and standing room. When it was completed in August, the new floodlights were inaugurated. The standing room in the south stand can accommodate about 1,200 guests, while the seating capacity is 4,500.

In August 2003, the stadium received a new video wall. Three years later, this was renewed again. The current scoreboard measures 9.23 by 6.78 meters.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-5)

During the 2007 summer break, a turf heating system was installed, new seats for the main stand were installed, and the old Block 1 was demolished. In the summer of 2008, the standing terraces of the north stand were roofed over. In addition, the corners between the counter stand and the adjoining blocks were closed off with media walls. A modular VIP building for 700 spectators was erected on the site of the former Block 1.

Since 2010, the entire stadium has been fitted with seats in the club colors of white and green, and the back straight bears the lettering _Kleeblatt_. The former main stand was given a new coat of paint. In 2011, the formerly colorful floodlights were painted white-green and fans redesigned the breakwaters and the entrance area of the north stand.

### Abandoned new stadium plans

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Abandoned new stadium plans")]

After interim plans to build a new stadium on the [Main-Danube Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main-Danube_Canal "Main-Danube Canal") in the south of the city, SpVgg Greuther Fürth extended its lease with the owner until 2040 in November 2012.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-6)

### Redevelopment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Redevelopment")]

In August 2015, the lease was extended another time, currently until 2050.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-7) At the same time, a decision was made to rebuild the main grandstand. The reconstruction took place in two phases: Phase 1, which included the demolition of the now 60-year-old main grandstand and a subsequent new construction with VIP stands, started in January 2016 and was completed by July 2017. To this end, the infrastructure around the stadium was also expanded away from the conversion of the grandstand. The previous training pitches behind the stadium were replaced by car parking spaces, for which a circular road was also drawn around the stadium. During the new construction, makeshift containers were used for changing rooms and media rooms, which were set up behind the back straight. Players entered the stadium through the open corner between the north stand and the back straight. In the second construction phase, which should have lasted until December 2017 but was delayed by several changes of architect and was not completed until the start of the 2017/18 season, the interior of the new main stand was fitted out. This provided the latter with meeting and conference rooms in addition to the infrastructure for the football events. These replaced the previous VIP North building, which had already been dismantled and sold. In its place, the main stand was extended to the north. The gap to the North Stand was closed before the 2018/19 season.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-8) It is still planned to extend the main stand to the south, which should thereby replace blocks A and B.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-9)

## Structure and facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Structure and facilities")]

After SpVgg Greuther Fürth's promotion to the Bundesliga in 2012, the south stand was rebuilt, increasing the stadium's capacity by 3,000 seats to 18,000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-10)

The south stand, where the away section is located, was completely roofed over.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-11) With the completion of the new main stand, the capacity decreased to 16,626 seats, as tickets are no longer sold in the adjacent blocks A and B in the south for reasons of visual obstruction. In total, there is room for 8,500 standing fans, slightly more than seats (8,126). The stadium is 100% covered.The capacity is divided as follows:

### Main stand

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Main stand")]

The main stand of the Ronhof is the heart of the stadium. After the old stand from 1951, as well as a temporal stand in front of it, were demolished, the club built a new grandstand with a revamped and vastly expanded VIP section, a new players' and match officials' area and a dedicated press space. Its internal area is used throughout the year for corporate events, as the different areas of the stand can be rented. The new stand has the same breadth as the old main stand. After its completion in 2017, the old VIP building to the north was demolished and a public grandstand in the same style as the new main stand was built, seating about 1,100 people and also functions as the home of the new club shop. Completed in summer 2018, the combined, completely covered, structure seats just under 2,700 spectators.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-12)

### North Stand

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: North Stand")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/2012-11-11_Fuerth2_%288208563665%29.jpg/250px-2012-11-11_Fuerth2_%288208563665%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2012-11-11_Fuerth2_(8208563665).jpg)

The North Stand

The North Stand is built as a terrace, and is home to the most vocal Fans of the "Kleeblatt". It was built in 1997 as a standing-room-only stand on the ground of the old, curved and which still functions as foundation to the stand. In 2008, the terrace along with the vestibule of the stand were covered with a roof, making it weatherproof. The north stand has room for 4,200 people in three sections, with Fürth's ultra groups finding their home in Block 3. Between the renovation 2008 and 2025, this section was split up to form a supporter-dedicated "Block 12", but due to the wish of the fans and the growth of their groups, this change has been reversed prior to the 2025/2026 season.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-13)

### Back straight

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Back straight")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Fuerth_Arena_Gegentribuene_2012-12-01.jpg/250px-Fuerth_Arena_Gegentribuene_2012-12-01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fuerth_Arena_Gegentribuene_2012-12-01.jpg)

The back straight in 2011.

Also built in 1997 to replace the old back straight with its legendary poplars, which fell victim to the reconstruction. It is a seating-only stand, seats approximately 3,000 people, and is the lowest stand in the stadium. Since 2018, there has been a beer garden behind it. In addition, the family block was moved from the south stand to the area of the back straight adjacent to the north stand.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-14)

### South End

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: South End")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Tag_HSV-Spiel.jpg/250px-Tag_HSV-Spiel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tag_HSV-Spiel.jpg)

View to the new South Stand, built in 2012

The new Südkurve (or south end) was also built after the promotion in 2012 in place of the old Südtribüne. In the process, the new stand was completely covered and provided with its own floodlights, since the roof restricts the light field of the floodlights. In front of blocks, A and B is a raised and covered platform with a ramp for wheelchair users. The only built-up curve in the stadium is occupied by the "Der Lohner" standing stand, which is named after the late former club president [Edgar Burkart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Burkart?action=edit&redlink=1 "Edgar Burkart (page does not exist)"), known as Lohner. Behind the goal, there is a seating grandstand, which is built somewhat lower in the area of the scoreboard. Adjacent to this is the away section, whose standing-room area has been carried over without change from the times before promotion. In total, the south stand can accommodate around 8,300 people. However, due to the new main stand being built approximately five meters closer to the pitch than before, the capacity of the south stand is restricted to about 6,700 people, as the sectors A and B as well as a part of the standing sector have no line of sight to the northern half of the pitch and are closed.

### Corners

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Corners")]

The corners of the stadium, with the exception of the southern corner on the side of the main stand, are currently not covered with stands. While there are two large advertising boards and the floodlight masts on the side of the back straight, there is a view from the entrance area of the North Stand between the North and Main Stands on the northern side of the Main Stand. There is also a floodlight mast here. There is also a passageway between the main stand and the south curve, so that it is theoretically possible to see a few square meters of the pitch from the street without a ticket.

## Name sponsorship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Name sponsorship")]

From 1997 to 2010, the Ronhof was officially called _Playmobil Stadium_. At that time, [Horst Brandstätter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horst_Brandst%C3%A4tter "Horst Brandstätter"), inventor and owner of [Playmobil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playmobil "Playmobil"), owned the stadium.

At the start of the 2010–11 season, [Mederer Süßwarenvertriebs GmbH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trolli "Trolli") (now Trolli GmbH) bought the naming rights to the stadium. Between July 2010 and June 2014, the stadium was thus called _Trolli Arena_.

From the expiration of the sponsorship agreement on July 1, 2014, until February 1, 2016, the _Ronhof_ temporarily bore the official name _Stadion am Laubenweg_.

In February 2016, it was renamed _Sportpark Ronhof | Thomas Sommer_. The new name is composed of the traditional name of the stadium and that of the Fürth-born real estate dealer _Thomas Sommer_, who became [Name Sponsor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sponsor_(commercial) "Sponsor (commercial)") until the summer of 2021.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-sportparkSommer-15) In August 2019, Sommer confirmed the extension of the sponsorship contract beyond 2021 and this regardless of the league. Per year, the contract brings SpVgg half a million euros.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-16) In November 2019, it was announced that the sponsorship agreement had been extended into 2025.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-17)

## Other uses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sportpark_Ronhof_Thomas_Sommer&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Other uses")]

The [Germany women's national football team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_women's_national_football_team "Germany women's national football team") has used the stadium for three international matches. The matches took place on September 23, 1999, against [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine_women's_national_football_team "Ukraine women's national football team"), on March 4, 2004, against [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_women's_national_football_team "China women's national football team"), and on April 8, 2015, against [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_women's_national_football_team "Brazil women's national football team").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpark_Ronhof#cite_note-18)

**Alexander Zorniger** (born 8 October 1967) is a German professional [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") manager who was most recently the head coach of [Danish Superliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Superliga "Danish Superliga") club [OB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odense_Boldklub "Odense Boldklub").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-1)

## Coaching career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Zorniger&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Coaching career")]

### Early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Zorniger&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early career")]

Zorniger started his coaching career with stints as head coach of [Normannia Gmünd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_Normannia_Gm%C3%BCnd "1. FC Normannia Gmünd"), assistant coach at [VfB Stuttgart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VfB_Stuttgart "VfB Stuttgart"), and as head coach at [Sonnenhof Großaspach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SG_Sonnenhof_Gro%C3%9Faspach "SG Sonnenhof Großaspach").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-2)

### RB Leipzig

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Zorniger&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: RB Leipzig")]

Zorniger became head coach of [RB Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RB_Leipzig "RB Leipzig") on 3 July 2012.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-Rangnick_entl%C3%A4sst_Pacult,_Zorniger_schon_da-3) He managed the club to an undefeated season in all competitions.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-RasenBallsport_Leipzig_-_Termine12%E2%80%9313-4) They finished the league season with 21 wins and 9 draws[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-5) and went on to the promotion play–off; winning the first leg 2–0 and drawing the second leg 2–2.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-RasenBallsport_Leipzig_-_Termine12%E2%80%9313-4) They also defeated [Chemnitzer FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemnitzer_FC "Chemnitzer FC") in the [Saxony Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxony_Cup "Saxony Cup") final.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-RasenBallsport_Leipzig_-_Termine12%E2%80%9313-4) He resigned on 11 February 2015, as earlier that month Ralf Rangnick announced that he would be RB Leipzig's coach for next season.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-Trainer_Zorniger_schmei%C3%9Ft_bei_RB_Leipzig_hin-6)

### Back to VfB Stuttgart

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Zorniger&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Back to VfB Stuttgart")]

On 25 May 2015, [VfB Stuttgart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VfB_Stuttgart "VfB Stuttgart") announced in a press conference that Zorniger would be their new head coach and signed a deal with the Swabians until Summer 2018.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-Alexander_Zorniger_neuer_Trainer_des_VfB_Stuttgart-7) He was sacked on 24 November 2015 after Stuttgart lost to [FC Augsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Augsburg "FC Augsburg") 4–0.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-VfB_Stuttgart_entl%C3%A4sst_Trainer_Zorniger-8) He finished with a record of five wins, one draw, and nine losses.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-VfB_Stuttgart_-_Trainerhistorie-9)

### Brøndby

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Zorniger&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Brøndby")]

On 17 May 2016, [Danish Superliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Superliga "Danish Superliga") club [Brøndby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%B8ndby_IF "Brøndby IF") announced that Zorniger had been appointed head coach on a two-year contract.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-Selskabsmeddelelse_14/2016:_Ny_cheftr%C3%A6ner-10) He made his competitive debut on 30 June with a 4–1 away win over Icelandic side [Valur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valur_men's_football "Valur men's football") in the first qualifying round of the [UEFA Europa League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_UEFA_Europa_League "2016–17 UEFA Europa League"), and Brøndby won the home leg 6–0 to advance 10–1 on aggregate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-11) On 17 July 2016, Zorniger oversaw his [Superliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Superliga "Danish Superliga") debut, a 4–0 home win against [Esbjerg fB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esbjerg_fB "Esbjerg fB").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-12) In the third qualifying round of the Europa League Brøndby eliminated [Hertha BSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertha_BSC "Hertha BSC") 3–2 on aggregate, overturning a 1–0 first-leg defeat in Berlin with a 3–1 victory at home.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-13) On 21 August Brøndby defeated [AGF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aarhus_Gymnastikforening "Aarhus Gymnastikforening") 7–0 at [Ceres Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_Park "Ceres Park"), the heaviest defeat in AGF's Superliga history,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-15) and a 1–1 home draw against rivals [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Copenhagen "FC Copenhagen") later that month sent Brøndby into the first international break of the season at the top of the table on goal difference.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-17) His first league defeat came on 18 September 2016 in a 2–1 home loss to [Viborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viborg_FF "Viborg FF").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-18)

Brøndby finished the [2016–17 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Danish_Superliga "2016–17 Danish Superliga") as runners-up, the club's highest league placing since 2005–06.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-19) The following season marked the peak of Zorniger's tenure. On 10 May 2018 Brøndby won the [Danish Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Cup "Danish Cup") with a 3–1 victory over [Silkeborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silkeborg_IF "Silkeborg IF") in the final, securing the club's first major trophy in 13 years.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-20) In the league, Brøndby led the table for long periods but, having been two goals ahead away to [Horsens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC_Horsens "AC Horsens") in the penultimate round, conceded twice in stoppage time to draw 2–2, a result that allowed Copenhagen to overtake them and win the title; Brøndby again finished second and missed out on what would have been their first championship since 2005.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-21)

During the [2018–19 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018%E2%80%9319_Danish_Superliga "2018–19 Danish Superliga") Brøndby were unable to reproduce their previous form and trailed the leading clubs in the Superliga. On 18 February 2019, with the team in third place following a home defeat to Esbjerg, the club announced that Zorniger had been relieved of his duties.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-22) According to sporting director [Ebbe Sand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebbe_Sand "Ebbe Sand"), the board no longer believed that he was the right coach to implement the club's long-term strategy, known as "Strategy 6.4", and felt that elements of the so-called "Brøndby DNA" were lacking in his playing style. Zorniger was also criticised in the Danish media and among some supporters for occasionally fielding starting line-ups consisting entirely of foreign players, which was seen by critics as conflicting with the club's ambition to develop home-grown talent.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-BT1-23)

### Apollon Limassol

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Zorniger&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Apollon Limassol")]

In December 2019, Zorniger was appointed head coach of [Apollon Limassol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollon_Limassol_FC "Apollon Limassol FC") in the [Cypriot First Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypriot_First_Division "Cypriot First Division").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-24) He led the club to the [2021–22](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Cypriot_First_Division "2021–22 Cypriot First Division") league title, Apollon's first championship in over a decade.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-25) After the club were eliminated in the third qualifying round of the [2022–23 UEFA Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_UEFA_Champions_League "2022–23 UEFA Champions League") in August 2022, he was dismissed.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-26)

### Greuther Fürth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Zorniger&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Greuther Fürth")]

After leaving Cyprus, Zorniger returned to Germany in October 2022 to take charge of Greuther Fürth.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-27) At the time, Fürth were bottom of the [2. Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2._Bundesliga "2. Bundesliga") with one of the youngest squads in the league, but Zorniger guided the team to ten points from his first four matches, lifting them to tenth place by the winter break. On 27 November 2023, with the club placed fifth, Fürth announced a contract extension with Zorniger until June 2026.

Following a poor run of form early in the [2024–25 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024%E2%80%9325_2._Bundesliga "2024–25 2. Bundesliga")—including five winless matches and a 4–0 defeat to [1. FC Nürnberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_N%C3%BCrnberg "1. FC Nürnberg")—the club dismissed both Zorniger and sporting director [Rachid Azzouzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachid_Azzouzi "Rachid Azzouzi") on 22 October 2024, with Fürth stating that they wished to take the team in a new direction.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-28)

### OB

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Zorniger&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: OB")]

On 31 May 2025, newly promoted [Danish Superliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Superliga "Danish Superliga") club [OB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odense_Boldklub "Odense Boldklub") announced that Zorniger would become their head coach for the [2025–26 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_Danish_Superliga "2025–26 Danish Superliga"), marking his return to Danish football more than six years after his departure from Brøndby.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-29)

Zorniger was dismissed on 30 July 2026, just one match into the [2026–27 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026%E2%80%9327_Odense_Boldklub_season?action=edit&redlink=1 "2026–27 Odense Boldklub season (page does not exist)"). OB stated that the decision was due to "collaboration difficulties and a lack of support for the club's direction and ambitions."[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-30)

## Style of management

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Zorniger&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Style of management")]

Zorniger's coaching philosophy is closely associated with the high-intensity pressing model developed in the [Red Bull football network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Bull_GmbH#Football "Red Bull GmbH"). During his time at [RB Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RB_Leipzig "RB Leipzig"), he typically used a narrow, vertical 4–4–2 or 4–2–2–2 system built around aggressive _[Gegenpressing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gegenpressing "Gegenpressing")_, rapid transitions and a high defensive line, with an emphasis on forcing mistakes rather than patient possession play.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-33) Analysts in Denmark later summarised his [Brøndby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%B8ndby_IF "Brøndby IF") philosophy with the phrase "create chaos, exploit chaos", reflecting his preference for attacking immediately after regaining possession and keeping the game at a high tempo.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-34)

At [VfB Stuttgart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VfB_Stuttgart "VfB Stuttgart") and Leipzig, Zorniger's teams were noted for some of the highest running and sprint metrics in their leagues and for committing large numbers forward in pressing and attacking phases, drawing comparisons in the German press with the approach of [Roger Schmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Schmidt_(footballer) "Roger Schmidt (footballer)").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-35) The same sources, however, also criticised his tactics as "naive" when the press was broken, highlighting the space left behind a very high back line and the vulnerability to counter-attacks if the collective movement and distances were not executed perfectly.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-36) This tension between attacking output and defensive exposure has been a recurring theme in media assessments of his work.

When he took over Brøndby in 2016, Zorniger imported the same high-pressure, transition-oriented style into the [Danish Superliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Superliga "Danish Superliga"). Brøndby's own season review described the approach with the slogan "Aktion, aktion, aktion", noting that training sessions under Zorniger were characterised by continuous activity and physical demands, with players required to jog or do push-ups between exercises.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-37) His Brøndby side quickly became known for a high tempo, aggressive counter-pressing and a direct attacking game that produced heavy wins and high scoring totals, but also attracted criticism for defensive instability and, at times, for fielding line-ups without any homegrown players, which some observers felt was at odds with the club's traditional identity and emphasis on youth development.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-38)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-BT1-23)

Later in his career, particularly at Greuther Fürth, reporting in Germany suggested a degree of evolution in Zorniger's approach. While _[kicker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kicker\_(sports\_magazine) "Kicker (sports magazine)")_ characterised his counter-pressing as the area where he remained "der Alte" ("the same as ever"), it also highlighted his focus on structuring a very young squad, improving defensive organisation and balancing his high-risk pressing game with greater stability.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-40) At Fürth he was also frequently portrayed as a demanding, outspoken motivator who expected high work-rate and resilience from his players, but who simultaneously spoke about shielding young footballers from external pressure and concentrating criticism and performance demands within the professional environment.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zorniger#cite_note-42)
